newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong shares firmer, Bangkok's bourse falls.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong shares firmer, Bangkok's bourse falls.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks gained on Monday as investors ignored a possible imminent rise in U.S. interest rates but Thailand's bourse was hit hard on concerns of who would take over the reins as the country's prime minister.
Elsewhere in Asia, Australian stocks slumped to a six-week low, and Singapore lost more than one percent.
Tokyo's market was closed for a national holiday.
Hong Kong's key Hang Seng index hit a new 1996 intra-day high, with investors hoping that any hike in interest rates by the U.S. Federal Reserve this week would be small.
The Fed's policy-setting body meets on Tuesday.

"There seem to be no concerns over the FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting. Most people have discounted a 25 basis point rise so they think that should be enough for the time being," said Frederick Tsang, head of research at PrimeEast Securities (HK) Ltd.
The Hang Seng closed 29.77 points or 0.26 percent higher at 11,622.13, after hitting a high for the year at 11,684.00.

"As long as rates don't go up by a significant amount, I think most investors have discounted the rise and people will focus on the fundamentals," Edward Chan, research director at NAVA SC Securities, said.
In Thailand, muted concern over the prospect of Thai Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh securing the premiership stripped 1.05 percent from the stock market.
The SET index ended the day down 11.01 points at 1,034.37.
"Investors sold on concerns that Chavalit would be appointed new prime minister," said Bumnan Liumsuwan of Asia Credit.

Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa announced on Saturday that he would step down within seven days as part of a deal with his coalition government partners for their backing in a censure motion against him.
Chavalit, leader of New Aspiration Party, has been tipped as the front runner to succeed Banharn.
"Investors are sceptical that Chavalit, if appointed, could solve economic problems...," said Bumnan.
The Australian share market closed at its lowest level in six weeks, hurt by continuing worries over base metal prices.
The All Ordinaries index fell 21.6 points or 0.96 percent to 2219.20.
Singapore's key share index was down 1.42 percent as blue chips fell on Friday's poor Singapore export figures and on a lack of institutional buyers.
The benchmark Straits Times Industrials index (STII) ended down 31.07 points or 1.42 percent at 2,156.79.
Friday's trade data showed a 6.3 percent year-on-year drop in non-oil exports in August.
Brokers in Seoul said the ongoing North Korean infiltration drama was not having a significant impact on the market.
The composite stock index closed up 0.83 point or 0.11 percent to a provisional 769.20.
A North Korean submarine ran aground close to the east coast city of Kangnung last Wednesday with an estimated 26 North Koreans on board.

Kuala Lumpur blue chips lost 0.36 percent, despite news that the long-awaited July trade figures were below the market's worst expectations. Malaysia recorded a trade gap of 624.5 million ringgit (US$249.8 million) for July.
The Composite Index ended down 4.09 points to 1,126.51.
Bombay shares ended lower in shaky trade as investors stayed away after former Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned as president of the Congress Party during the weekend.
At 1102 GMT, the dollar was at 109.84/9.94 yen and 1.5162/67 marks.
Bullion ended at US$381.00/381.50, against New York's US$380.85/381.25 close on Friday.
SIMEX North Sea Brent crude oil futures for November were indicated slightly firmer in late trading. November rose six cents to $22.05 a barrel against Friday's London settle of $21.99.
